crime.value: Murder(s) in a small Civil War-era town: Eddie Larsen vanishes after drunkenly going to steal cider, with only blood on rocks and no corpse; central question is what happened to the body and who really killed him. A second body, Dink O'Day, is later found stuffed in a barrel.
crime.quote: I'm arrested for the murder, for which they have not even found a corpse

victim.value: Eddie Larsen, a drunk young man killed trespassing to steal cider from Jack Mattick's shed; and Dink O'Day, Mattick's accomplice who tried to blackmail him
victim.quote: Mattick had caught Eddie Larsen in his shed trying to steal some cider and had lit out after him with a rifle.

closed_world.value: The small town of Capstone and its outskirts — jail, Dooley House, Gibson's tavern, the marsh, Mattick's farm and Shantytown — a tight community where everyone knows everyone
closed_world.quote: Pete was the only one in Capstone who owned a hat like that

culprit_and_motive.value: Jack Mattick: shot Eddie Larsen for stealing cider, sold the body to a grave-robbing doctor for cadaver money, then strangled Dink O'Day when Dink blackmailed him
culprit_and_motive.quote: he had choked Dink to death and then... he decided he might as well sell Dink's remains to the doctor too

resolution.value: The boys' night search of Mattick's shed uncovers Dink's body in a barrel and the buried empty coffin; Sheriff Rice arrests Mattick, who confesses. Jimmy Grover is exonerated and the reward is paid for his safe return.
resolution.quote: "He buried an empty box, Mattick did," I said.

investigator.value: Two boys — narrator Gascius (an outsider child witness) and his fearless, scheming friend Pete Mariah — amateur juvenile investigators driven by curiosity
investigator.quote: "You just meet me, Gascius," he said. "Ten o'clock, at the crossroads."

suspect_architecture.value: Small-town cast: Jimmy Grover, the drunkard convicted on circumstantial evidence (means/opportunity: last seen arguing with Eddie Larsen); Jack Mattick, the shady farmer whose shed Eddie went to rob (real killer, motive: protecting property and then silencing a blackmailer); Dink O'Day, Mattick's accomplice who becomes a second victim; a body-snatching doctor in Little Village as accessory. Differentiation is by reputation — the town's disreputables are presumed guilty.
suspect_architecture.quote: "But everybody says you're a murderer," Pete said stubbornly

red_herring.value: The public quarrel between Jimmy and Eddie witnessed by the Misses Tabers and Doctor Howell, plus the blood marks on the rocks near the road and Jimmy's drunkenness (suggesting a blackout killing) — all pointing to Jimmy. Also the empty coffin buried at Dink O'Day's funeral, which initially seems to hide Eddie's body.
red_herring.quote: "But lots of blood marks on the rocks near the road," Pete said.

clue_fairness.value: Fair: the reader is told in Jimmy's own account that Eddie went to steal cider from Mattick's shed; the empty buried box, the missing corpse, the doctor known to buy cadavers, and Mattick's dubious Shantytown wealth are all presented before the boys find Dink in the barrel and before the confession.
clue_fairness.quote: "He buried an empty box, Mattick did," I said.

social_world.value: Civil-War-era village of Capstone: respectable townsfolk (storekeepers, farmers, Dooley House men) versus Shantytown disreputables; the sheriff holds badge-authority; Eddie Larsen's father commands opinion through a $200 reward; reputation determines guilt, and a grave-robbing doctor's money sustains a hidden economy.
social_world.quote: he was something of a dubious character who associated in Shantytown a lot

alibi.value: Jimmy's only account is his own uncorroborated story — he says he parted from Eddie, who reeled off toward Mattick's; no witness supports him, and two days pass unaccounted for. Mattick's implicit cover is that he was uninvolved, undone by the lit window and his call for 'the doctor'.
alibi.quote: "The last I saw of him he was reeling down the road to Mattick's place."

reveal_mechanic.value: Physical discovery plus a verbal slip: the boys find Dink O'Day's body stuffed in a canvas-covered barrel in Mattick's shed (proving the buried coffin was empty), and Mattick, mistaking the sheriff for his visitor, calls out 'Is that you, doctor?' — exposing the cadaver-selling trade; full confession follows in the jail.
reveal_mechanic.quote: he said out, "Is that you, doctor?"

media_and_audience.value: Town gossip functions as the press: 'everybody says you're a murderer', the hanging is treated as settled fact and folklore ('bad luck to be looked at by somebody who is going to be hanged'), and a mob forms with a dead-or-alive bounty; at the end the same public voice reverses into an apology.
media_and_audience.quote: "It has just occurred to me, gentlemen, we all owe Jimmy Grover an apology."

investigator_wound.value: The boy narrator Gascius is torn between conscience and cowardice — fearful of consequences, unable to lie like Pete, weighed down by guilt at the thought of watching a man hang because of him; Pete's wound is greed for the reward warring with his sense of Jimmy's innocence.
investigator_wound.quote: A little bit of trumped-up disbelief can go a long way in mitigating a nervous conscience

victims_enemies.value: Eddie Larsen, a drunk thief, made enemies by trespassing: he was caught stealing cider from Jack Mattick, a dubious Shantytown-connected farmer with a fierce temper; the second victim, Dink O'Day, was Mattick's own accomplice who turned blackmailer.
victims_enemies.quote: Mattick had caught Eddie Larsen in his shed trying to steal some cider and had lit out after him with a rifle.

suspect_wounds.value: Jimmy Grover's drunkenness is his vulnerability: he was the last man seen with Eddie, had publicly cuffed and quarreled with him, and was drunk enough that the town can claim he killed without remembering.
suspect_wounds.quote: “They say you was awful drunk and did it without knowing and that now you don’t remember,” Pete said.

unreliable_frame.value: The narrator is a boy, Gascius, recounting events colored by superstition and childish fear; his companion Pete is a practiced liar ('he could turn mighty artful'), and Jimmy's protestation of innocence is exactly what a guilty man would say, as Pete notes.
unreliable_frame.quote: “He says he is, of course, but I don’t suppose he’d have much trouble influencing himself of that.”

setting_as_constraint.value: Tiny Civil War-era town of Capstone: everyone knows everyone, every horse is commandeered for the manhunt so a fugitive cannot flee, and the isolated Mattick farm near the marsh plus nearby Little Village and lawless Shantytown make body-disposal and body-selling possible unobserved.
setting_as_constraint.quote: Most everybody who had a horse was mounted and so there wasn’t an idle horse about at all.

evidence_type.value: Physical discovery: Dink O'Day's corpse stuffed in a canvas-covered barrel in Mattick's shed, corroborated by the buried empty coffin box and Mattick's slip asking for the doctor.

false_suspect.value: Jimmy Grover, condemned to hang for Eddie Larsen's murder on circumstantial testimony despite no corpse being found.
false_suspect.quote: “I’m arrested for the murder, for which they have not even found a corpse. . .”

technical_detail.value: The trade in cadavers: a doctor in Little Village known to rob graves would buy bodies for research, so Mattick could dispose of corpses for profit and bury an empty coffin at the funeral — the empty box being what exposes him.
technical_detail.quote: sold the doctor the body (the doctor was known to rob graves to get cadavers to do research on)

moral_ambiguity.value: Pete, the boy hero, nearly sells the man he rescued for the two-hundred-dollar reward, rationalizing it as likely justice; the town's murderous certainty and even Larsen's reward for a hanging show ordinary people willing to kill on conclusion rather than evidence.
moral_ambiguity.quote: “But it ain’t right to hang a man for what people happen to conclude,” Jimmy said hotly.
